item.title: FIBA secretary general addresses why organization hasn't added 'men's' label to flagship World Cup event
item.description: FIBA's Andreas Zagklis linked the World Cup naming debate to ongoing transgender eligibility questions about who can compete in men's and women's events.
item.content:encoded:
FIBA Secretary General Andreas Zagklis addressed the organization’s decision not to formally label its flagship global tournament the "Men’s Basketball World Cup," connecting the naming debate to broader questions about eligibility in men’s and women’s competitions.

"The naming is of course a matter that the Central Board has discussed," Zagklis told reporters Sunday during a press conference ahead of the 2026 FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup. "The Central Board has for the moment maintained the current naming. We do not see that the aspect of men’s and women’s is something that devalues or values the other World Cup in such a way."

FIBA officially calls its women’s tournament the "FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup." Its other senior five-on-five tournament remains the "FIBA Basketball World Cup," without "men’s" in the title. Zagklis added that the organization is also considering "broader concerns" over the separation of the men's and women's categories, and referenced studies over "who can compete" in each respective competition.

FIBA SECRETARY GENERAL ANDREAS ZAGKLIS SPEAKS OUT ON CAITLIN CLARK'S IMPACT ON GROWTH OF WORLD CUP

"We also need to be cognizant of the broader concerns about men and women, and the concerns as well as the studies we are making for our competition and who can compete in the women’s World Cup and who can compete in the other World Cup, which is not necessarily just the men’s World Cup," he said.

Zagklis did not explicitly mention transgender athletes in his answer. However, FIBA has publicly confirmed that it is reviewing transgender eligibility and has established an interim approach while that process continues.

Following the International Olympic Committee’s adoption of a policy protecting the female category, the FIBA Central Board confirmed in April that FIBA will follow the IOC standard for the Olympic and Youth Olympic Games. The federation said it is waiting for further guidance on the practical, legal and operational aspects of implementation.

FIBA-run competitions, including its World Cups, remain subject to a separate review. In December 2024, the Central Board extended its process for adopting a formal transgender eligibility policy by two years.

FIBA said it is collecting basketball-specific data and evidence related to transgender participation. A Gender Eligibility Committee composed of medical and legal experts is scheduled to give the Central Board its recommendations at the beginning of 2027.

Until then, FIBA said it will not entertain transgender eligibility requests. The organization therefore has not announced a permanent policy for its own competitions, but transgender applicants cannot receive eligibility approval while the review remains underway.

Zagklis' answers come amid ongoing controversy in the WNBA, which operates under a different set of rules.

The WNBA’s collective bargaining agreement says only women may play in the league. However, it does not publicly define that term or provide specific eligibility standards for transgender or intersex players.

Debate intensified after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham supported excluding transgender women and girls from female sports. Her comments prompted demonstrations supporting and opposing transgender participation outside WNBA games.

WNBA COMMISSIONER CATHY ENGELBERT SENDS TRANS INCLUSION MEMO AFTER ENES FREEDOM, ROYCE WHITE ANNOUNCEMENTS

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White later declared themselves eligible for a future WNBA draft after publicly identifying themselves as women. Their announcements were widely viewed as attempts to challenge the wording of the league’s eligibility rule.

A WNBA task force discussed the subject in August but did not adopt a new standard. The league said no immediate eligibility matter affected the WNBA and condemned "bad-faith" efforts to demean or marginalize others.

Supporters of sex-based eligibility rules argue that clear boundaries protect fairness and opportunities in women’s sports. Supporters of transgender inclusion argue that blanket restrictions can discriminate against a small and frequently targeted population.

Unlike the WNBA, FIBA has announced a formal review, created an expert committee and established a timeline for recommendations. But it has not disclosed the evidence collected so far or indicated what policy it may ultimately adopt.

Zagklis’ remarks did not announce a new rule. They showed that FIBA’s decision to leave "men’s" out of its World Cup name exists alongside a continuing discussion about how the organization will define eligibility for both competitions.

When asked about the nature and purpose of the studies Zagklis was referring to and whether FIBA would anticipate biological males competing in the next FIBA Women's World Cup, FIBA pointed OutKick to the Central Board meeting back in April before the tournament began.

item.title: Champion athlete soils herself mid-race and keeps going, prompting fitness competition to change rules
item.description: HYROX Beijing 2026 winner Joanna Wietrzyk faced online backlash after an incontinence incident during the race, prompting new competition rule changes.
item.content:encoded:
A popular global fitness competition is changing its rules after an explosive incident at a Sept. 12 competition.

Australian professional athlete Joanna Wietrzyk won the race at HYROX Beijing — but the victory did not come without struggle.

During the race, Wietrzyk experienced fecal incontinence but continued competing. Despite the incident, judges and officials did not instruct her to stop, prompting concerns about potential health and safety risks for other competitors.

'A WIN IS A WIN' SAYS ATHLETE WHO DIDN'T LET A LITTLE DIARRHEA KEEP HER FROM FINISHING IN FIRST PLACE

The incident has sparked online debate — some people have supported Wietrzyk for her perseverance, while others suggested that her accident posed a potential biohazard.

Wietrzyk reportedly addressed the incident in a social media post, which has since been deleted.

"Go hard or go home … a win is a win. In all seriousness, thank you for all the support. I’ll be back soon x," she wrote, according to multiple news outlets.

COULD 'HUMANMAXXING' ACTUALLY HELP YOU LIVE LONGER? HERE'S WHAT EXPERTS SAY

The athlete has since faced criticism from those who argue that her decision posed a health risk to other competitors.

Wietrzyk’s coach, Chris Bayens, posted a statement on social media in her defense. "What happened was an extraordinary set of circumstances that were unforeseen, rapidly evolving and almost impossible to fully comprehend in real time," he wrote on Instagram.

"Decisions were made under competition conditions by an athlete, judges and officials, all responding to a situation none of them could reasonably have prepared for."

Bayens continued that these decisions can be reviewed and lessons can be learned, but "judging someone’s intent, character or morality through the clarity of hindsight is neither fair nor honest."

FITNESS EXPERT VISITS GYMS NATIONWIDE, SHOUTS OUT 4 CLUBS FOR 'GETTING IT RIGHT'

"Sport occasionally produces moments that are imperfect and deeply human," he said. "Discussion is legitimate. The hatred and personal attacks that have followed are not."

Moritz Furste, co-founder of HYROX, also released a statement following the incident.

"I apologize to all that were directly or indirectly affected, as well as to everyone who felt like we did not handle the situation like we should have," he wrote. "HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end, it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not."

FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS SIMPLE RULE TO GET IN SHAPE WITHOUT DREADING THE GYM: 'JUST MOVE'

The statement continued, "Of course, we started improving event processes, plus making rulebook changes immediately. As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again. We learn and try to get better every day."

According to HYROX, the race combines cardio with weight training, involving a total of eight kilometers (about five miles) of running and eight functional workout stations.

The structure of the competitions layers a one-kilometer run with one functional workout station, including SkiErg (a machine that simulates cross-country skiing), sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jumps, rowing, farmers carry, sandbag lunges and wall balls.

Launched in Germany in 2017, HYROX has grown rapidly worldwide, with recent reports putting participation at more than 1.4 million competitors globally. The organization describes the race as the world's fastest-growing fitness sport.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

More than 98% of HYROX competitors complete the race, with no time limit to finish and no qualification required to enter.

"The structure of HYROX eliminates the generic fear of ‘coming last,’" the brand wrote on its website.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, California-based certified fitness trainer Ryan Read shared why the HYROX format can be so physically demanding.

"Your body doesn't get much time to fully recover between efforts," he said. "You may go from running directly to sled pushes, lunges or rowing. That forces your heart, lungs and muscles to work hard for a long period."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As the race progresses, maintaining proper form can become more difficult, according to Read, as the combination of intensity, duration and repetitive exercises can put a "significant amount of stress on the body."

"Muscles become fatigued and the body uses up stored energy and fluids," he said. "During hard exercise, more blood is directed toward working muscles and away from the digestive system. That can make digestion more difficult."

Running in particular creates a repetitive movement that can upset the stomach. Combining this with dehydration, heat and eating too close to competition can worsen symptoms, Read cautioned.

"This is why some athletes experience nausea, cramping, diarrhea or even vomiting during endurance events."

There is a "big difference" between working through normal discomfort and ignoring a medical warning sign, according to the trainer.

Elite athletes are often conditioned to push through pain, a mindset that can intensify during competition. Adrenaline can also make it harder to recognize when the body is in distress, Read said.

Symptoms like vomiting, fainting, severe chest pain or extreme weakness "should not be treated as proof that someone is working hard enough."

"Pushing through certain symptoms can turn a manageable problem into a medical emergency," he emphasized. "Real toughness also means knowing when your body is telling you to stop."

Read suggested that fitness organizations should have "clear rules" for when an athlete needs to be evaluated or removed from a competition, and medical staff should be easily accessible throughout the event.

"Equipment that becomes contaminated with vomit, blood or other bodily fluids should be taken out of use immediately," he said. "Simply wiping it quickly and sending the next competitor through may not be enough."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Bodily fluids can contain germs that may spread through contaminated surfaces or direct contact, Read said.

"The exact risk depends on the fluid, organism and type of exposure. Competitor safety should come before keeping the event moving on schedule."

item.title: President John Quincy Adams knew one book people needed to read to become good citizens
item.description: John Quincy Adams wrote letters urging his son to read the Bible daily, believing Scripture was essential to raising citizens worthy of the Constitution.
item.content:encoded:
Too few American students know enough about our Constitution. Still, fewer know there is such a thing as "Constitution Day." But this year, it might be worth taking up an assignment our sixth president gave to his son in a remarkable series of letters written while President John Quincy Adams served as minister to Russia.

Adams did not focus on career advice for his son. He did not teach his son how to make money.

Instead, Adams insisted upon this: Read the Bible. Every day.

BILL BENNETT: WHAT I TOLD MY SONS ABOUT THEIR FAITH, FAMILY AND AMERICA

Adams believed no education could be complete without it. He wrote to his son that when "duly read and meditated on," the Bible is "of all books in the world, that which contributes most to make men good, wise, and happy."

And here’s where our Constitution comes in: Adams believed children formed by Scripture would become "useful citizens to their country" and "respectable members of society."

GORSUCH HIGHLIGHTS STAGGERING DECLINE IN CIVIC LITERACY THAT PROMPTED HIM TO AUTHOR NEW BOOK

There’s much ado today about civics education. And that’s a good thing. More educators and parents should ask: Should students memorize the Constitution? Learn about the three branches of government? Study the Federalist Papers? All extremely important.

But John Quincy Adams understood something too many have largely forgotten.

AMERICA’S NEXT 250 YEARS DEPEND ON PASSING FAITH AND FREEDOM TO OUR CHILDREN

The Constitution details how we, a free people, govern ourselves. But it cannot teach rising generations how to become worthy of that freedom.

That is why Adams spent letter after letter introducing his son to the New Testament and to the Hebrew Bible — to Genesis, Exodus, the Ten Commandments and to the Law of Moses. He argued the Mosaic Law represented the greatest moral revolution of the ancient world because it united justice with humanity.

TEN COMMANDMENTS BELONG IN TEXAS SCHOOLS AND THE SUPREME COURT CAN PROTECT THEM

Unlike the legal systems of Greece and Rome, which largely emphasized civic order or individual virtue, Adams believed the Hebrew Scriptures taught something unprecedented: Duties toward other people were also duties toward God. The laws protecting the stranger, the widow, the orphan and even enemies reflect a moral vision unlike anything the secular world had produced.

Adams admired the Hebrew Bible because it did something no human legislature could accomplish.

THE BEDROCK OF AMERICAN LIBERTY WAS LAID IN JERUSALEM

It recognized individual merit and responsibility. It legislated for human nature.

Governments can punish theft. They cannot eliminate envy. Governments can outlaw murder. They cannot command honor, gratitude, humility or self-control.

John Quincy Adams’s letters were never simply about raising his own successful children. They were about transmitting civilization itself to all America’s children.

Too many fathers today have outsourced the most important conversations about duty, morality and character to schools, to government institutions, to coaches or even to celebrities. Mothers play an indispensable role in raising virtuous children, but there is no substitute for the unique influence of an engaged father who teaches his son what it means to be an honorable man.

DADS AREN’T OPTIONAL — AND AMERICA’S KIDS ARE PAYING THE BRUTAL PRICE

The consequences of absence are all around us.

Young Americans increasingly struggle to distinguish rights from responsibilities. They know how to demand respect but not always how to earn it. They have been taught self-esteem more often than self-government. They build professional résumés but little aptitude for disappointment, mental resilience or for duty.

ALEX BERENSON: GENTLE PARENTING CAN'T REPLACE THE STRENGTH OF A GOOD DAD

This isn't merely an educational, civic or cultural problem. It's a fatherhood problem.

For centuries, American fathers understood that one of their highest callings was to introduce their children to the moral inheritance that made liberty possible.

Not because government required it. Because freedom required it.

The Hebrew Bible teaches children human beings are capable of both good and evil. Actions have consequences. Morality matters. And it importantly teaches every person bears the image of God.

The Founders knew constitutions cannot preserve themselves. Republics depend upon citizens capable of governing themselves before they presume to govern others.

John Quincy Adams understood this better than most. His letters to his son were, in many ways, one manual for raising a free citizen.

Perhaps that is the lesson we most need today: If we want stronger schools, we need stronger families. If we want better citizens, we need fathers who teach virtues.

If we want to renew American civics, we should certainly continue teaching the Constitution.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

But we should also recover the book John Quincy Adams believed came first: The Bible.

Because before America can produce good presidents, good judges or good citizens, it must first produce men and women of character.

item.title: Homeowners in the heart of America’s AI boom are getting an unexpected payoff
item.description: Loudoun County homeowners save $5,800 a year in property taxes thanks to data centers, which generate 45% of all local tax revenue on just 3% of land.
item.content:encoded:
Billions in build-outs of facilities to support the artificial intelligence (AI) boom have become a lightning rod in communities across America, but homeowners in the nation’s data center capital are seeing a surprising payoff — thousands of dollars in property tax relief.

The massive projects have emerged as an issue in the 2026 midterm elections, as voters raise concerns about electricity costs, water use, land development and the strain on local infrastructure. Opposition has crossed party lines, forcing candidates to confront an industry that state and local governments spent years courting.

Yet just outside Washington, D.C., the richest U.S. enclave of Loudoun County, Virginia, offers a striking case study of the industry's economic upside.

Home to the sprawling tech corridor known as "Data Center Alley," Loudoun has the highest concentration of data centers in the world. Decades of development have transformed the county's landscape and dramatically expanded its tax base, offering a real-world look at the financial benefits proponents say the industry can bring to local communities.

8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS

"Loudoun County has more data centers than anywhere else in the country. It's been sort of the capital of data center development for decades," Jared Walczak, vice president of state projects at the Tax Foundation, told Fox News Digital.

"And because of that, Loudoun County property taxes are about half of what they would be without data centers. In fact, data centers provide about 45% of all local tax revenue to Loudoun County, not just property taxes, but all local tax revenue."

Walczak said the impact translates into significant savings for individual homeowners.

"The average homeowner would pay $5,800 more a year in property taxes if you didn't have data center development," he said, noting that data centers occupy only about 3% of the county's land.

But the rapid expansion of data centers has also fueled concerns that their enormous electricity demands could leave residents footing a higher utility bill, potentially offsetting some of those savings.

THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS

Walczak pushed back on that worry, arguing the industry's impact on homeowners' property taxes is clearer.

"The property tax relief is real, measurable, and significant," he said. "The energy costs are largely a solved problem."

Walczak told Fox News Digital that the increased demand could require utilities to build new generation and transmission infrastructure, while adding more customers and electricity usage can also spread the grid's fixed costs across a larger base.

The critical question, he said, is who pays for the additional infrastructure.

"You pay for the additional generation and transmission capacity. The data center pays for that," Walczak said. "And then you actually see a slight reduction in energy costs for everyone."

He pointed again to Northern Virginia, arguing that its experience challenges fears that a heavy concentration of data centers inevitably translates into higher electricity prices for residents.

"If you look at the places with the largest data center development, you actually see declines in energy prices relative to the rest of the country," Walczak said. "You look at Northern Virginia, it has lower energy prices."

As communities across the country weigh the costs and benefits of the data center boom, Walczak said Loudoun County's experience offers a glimpse at what can happen when billions of dollars in new infrastructure become part of the local tax base.

item.title: Ridiculous USA Today column proves that the demand for misogyny in sports far exceeds the supply
item.description: A USA Today columnist cited Sydney Sweeney's betting ad, an Arch Manning joke and an arena rendering as proof sports don't want women around.
item.content:encoded:
The demand for misogyny in American sports far exceeds the available supply.

That's a problem for USA Today columnist Nancy Armour.

Armour has built much of her professional brand around finding sexism and misogyny everywhere she looks in sports. So, what happens when women reach a better position in the sports world than ever before?

Armour has to look harder.

Much harder.

In a column published Tuesday, Armour argued that American sports are happy to take women's money, but don't want women in their space or to treat them with "even the slightest shred of decency."

Strong claim.

What evidence did Armour use to support the idea that American sports, as a whole, don't want women around?

A sports-betting ad featuring a nearly nude Sydney Sweeney, Arch Manning laughing at a stupid AI video, and an architectural rendering that included almost no women.

That's it. That's her entire case.

The arena rendering barely warrants a response. An architectural rendering of Philadelphia’s future arena showed almost no women, the image was replaced within two days, and the building will be home to the city’s WNBA team. If that is evidence that women aren’t welcome in sports, the definition of evidence has lost all meaning.

There's another problem, though. Armour has no trouble finding misogyny in an advertisement, a joke or a computer-generated crowd. But when males take opportunities in women's sports, she attacks the women who object.

That's not an oversight. It's the clearest evidence that this isn't really about protecting women.

Armour starts with perhaps the most absurd characterization of the three.

"A betting company tells women their only place in sports is as a sexualized object," Armour wrote.

Wait, when did Novig say that?

It didn't.

Novig produced one advertisement featuring one woman, Sydney Sweeney, using sex appeal to promote a sports prediction market. Somehow, Armour took that to mean the company declared that every woman's "only place in sports" is as a sexualized object.

That's quite a leap.

The ad didn't say anything about female athletes, female fans, female broadcasters or women's sports. Plus, Novig isn't selling "sports." Sports are the subject matter. The product is gambling.

And the ad is clearly designed primarily to appeal to men, who make up the core audience for sports betting.

So what?

Not every product or advertisement has to appeal equally to men and women. Women’s clothing companies and cosmetics companies run ads aimed at women. Entire television networks and publishing genres cater primarily to women. No one treats that as evidence that those companies hate men.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

But when a betting company creates an ad tailored to its overwhelmingly male audience, Armour treats the existence of a male audience as the offense.

In Armour's world, products aimed at women are called empowerment, while products aimed at men are called misogyny.

Then there's Sweeney's role in all of this. According to Novig CEO Jacob Fortinsky, Sweeney approached the company, owns equity in it and drove much of the campaign's "visuals and messaging."

In other words, an adult woman made a business decision to use her own image to promote a company in which she has a financial interest.

Armour responded by calling the ad misogynistic, effectively condemning Sweeney for exercising that agency in a way that appeals to men.

Apparently, women are free to make their own choices, provided Nancy Armour approves of them.

NIKE-LINKED COACHINGHER PROGRAM FACES SCRUTINY OVER GENDER BIAS TRAINING AND DEFINITION OF GIRLS

Armour later claimed that Novig "backpedaled" on its "misogyny." That's not even true.

Fortinsky publicly defended the campaign, credited Sweeney with driving the concept and said the company was pleased with the response. Incredibly, Armour linked the word "backpedaled" to a story whose headline said the Novig CEO "defends" the ad.

Armour anticipated that someone might point out that female athletes have posed nude for magazines, including ESPN’s famous "Body Issue." She insisted those examples are different because the athletes’ bodies were "the product of years of work and training" and should be appreciated for their accomplishments rather than "ogled over for sexual gratification."

Huh.

So Armour has appointed herself the arbiter of which women have bodies worthy of being displayed and which women are merely objects. Female athletes who pose nude receive her approval because their nudity serves an Armour-approved purpose.

Sweeney voluntarily used her own sex appeal to promote a company she partly owns, and Armour branded her decision misogynistic because it was meant to appeal to men.

Careful, Nancy. Deciding which women’s bodies are worthy of being seen and which aren’t sounds awfully misogynistic.

Armour’s second example comes from a press conference after Texas’ comeback victory over Ohio State.

Manning was asked whether he had seen any fan-edited clips from the game. He said he had seen an AI edit of Sarkisian’s postgame interview, then volunteered the specific clip.

"Of him slapping Holly Rowe?" Manning said, laughing. "It’s hilarious."

The AI video grew out of an awkward exchange after the game. Rowe attempted to interview Sarkisian moments after Texas completed a 20-point comeback and delivered one of the biggest victories of his career. Sarkisian shouted "Texas fight," flashed the Hook ’em sign and left to celebrate with his team.

Rowe responded by throwing up her hands, rolling her eyes and walking off in a huff.

Texas later said technical problems with ESPN’s equipment contributed to the failed interview. Similar problems had disrupted an attempted interview at halftime, but in that instance, ESPN’s Laura Rutledge explained that Sarkisian had waited patiently and said the network owed him an apology.

So, what exactly did Manning do wrong? He laughed at a fake video making fun of this ridiculous scene.

No woman was assaulted and Manning clearly wasn’t laughing at actual violence. He reacted honestly to an obviously fake parody of an awkward postgame exchange.

Sports media members constantly complain that athletes are boring, guarded and coached to speak in clichés. Then an athlete offers one unfiltered reaction, and those same media members treat it as evidence of a deep moral failing.

This is exactly why athletes never say anything interesting.

Manning quickly learned the lesson. He issued the kind of carefully written, corporate apology that public figures release when honesty becomes more trouble than it’s worth. He apologized publicly, spoke privately with Rowe and received her forgiveness.

Rowe could have ended the entire controversy by saying no apology was necessary. Instead, she publicly accepted Manning’s apology and referenced their private conversation. That allowed her to occupy both of the most powerful positions in this particular media ecosystem: the victim who had been wronged and the gracious authority willing to offer forgiveness.

Victimhood is power in this world, and the more of it you can claim, the better.

REPORTER FOR THE ATHLETIC FUMES OVER ARCH MANNING, SILENT ON JOSH JACOBS' ALLEGED VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMAN

Plus, accountability only flows in one direction when someone is permanently cast as the victim. Everyone else must apologize to Rowe. Rowe never has to apologize for her own behavior, which included an incredibly petty on-camera reaction.

But even after Rowe accepted Manning’s apology, that wasn’t enough for Armour.

She wrote that Manning’s apology "doesn’t matter" because "the damage was done."

Then what, exactly, would matter?

Manning apologized publicly and privately. Armour still refused to let the incident end because resolution is useless to someone who needs permanent victims.

The misogyny boat must stay afloat.

To connect these three completely unrelated episodes, Armour turned to Purdue professor Cheryl Cooky.

"It's about a reinscribing of those spaces and a reassertion of those sports as male-dominated and masculine-oriented institutions," Cooky told Armour.

She added that when women gain power, society responds with a backlash.

Well, there you have it. Two people subscribe to Armour's theory.

Unfortunately, neither provided any evidence that these three incidents were part of a backlash against women gaining power.

Did Manning laugh at a dumb AI video because he felt threatened by women gaining power? Did Sweeney create a sexually provocative gambling ad to punish female athletes for becoming more popular? Did whoever populated an architectural rendering with men do so as an act of resistance against the WNBA?

Armour doesn't even attempt to prove any of that.

The study Armour cited, co-authored by Cooky, examined the amount and quality of coverage women's sports received on selected television news and highlight programs during three sampling periods in 2024.

Whatever someone thinks of that research, it doesn't establish the motives of Sweeney, Manning or the person who populated an architectural rendering.

Cooky's contribution amounts to translating Armour's argument into academic jargon. "Male-dominated and masculine-oriented institutions" sounds more authoritative than "men don't want us here," but it doesn't make the claim true.

Armour didn't find proof; she found a professor willing to repeat her conclusion so the same opinion could be presented as expertise.

The most revealing aspect of Armour's misogyny hustle isn't where she claims to find misogyny.

It's the one place where she refuses to see it.

In 2023, then-ESPN host Sam Ponder argued that women deserve fair, sex-based athletic competition. Armour responded with an 800-word attack and accused Ponder of using "fairness" to cloak her "bigotry toward transgender girls and women."

"What ESPN's Sam Ponder calls 'fairness' is plain old bigotry," Armour's headline read.

Got that?

According to Armour, an architectural rendering, an advertisement starring Sydney Sweeney and an off-the-cuff remark by Arch Manning are major threats to women in sports. But a male athlete taking a roster spot, playing time, trophies or championships from girls and women isn't a threat.

Worse than that, Armour attacks the women who object to those males.

Careful, Nancy. You're starting to sound awfully misogynistic again.

Look at the women Armour chooses to attack: Sydney Sweeney, Sam Ponder and Riley Gaines. They are strong, successful women exercising their own agency, and Armour turns on them the moment they make choices she doesn’t like.

That's Nancy Armour's brand in a nutshell: men are responsible for everything wrong with women's sports, except the men who "identify" as women. Those men must be defended, even if doing so requires tearing down women like Ponder and Gaines.

Armour can hold both positions because she isn’t applying a consistent principle about protecting women. She’s applying whatever progressive ideology demands at that particular moment.

LEFT-WING SPORTS HOST SARAH SPAIN LAUNCHES DISGUSTING PERSONAL SMEAR OF SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM

Sweeney voluntarily uses her own sex appeal to promote a company she partly owns? Complicit in misogyny.

Ponder voluntarily defends women’s athletic opportunities? Bigot.

Perfect.

The strangest part of Armour's column is that she spends several paragraphs undermining her own argument.

She acknowledges that women's sports have "never been more popular" and female athletes have "never had more visibility." She notes that WNBA TV ratings, franchise values and salaries are soaring. She points to signature Nike lines for Caitlin Clark and A'ja Wilson, women coaching in the NFL and NBA, merchandise designed specifically for female fans, women's sports bars and teams building their own stadiums.

That sounds like incredible progress.

Because it is.

Women have more opportunities, influence, visibility and economic power in sports than at any point in American history. The evidence no longer supports declaring that American sports refuse to treat women with "the slightest shred of decency."

So, Armour takes three minor and unrelated examples, assigns all of them the same sweeping motive and tells readers that the "male sports monopoly" is lashing out against powerful women.

Essentially, the demand for misogyny now far exceeds the supply.

And that's a major problem for people whose relevance depends on convincing women that they're still surrounded by it.

Armour ended her column by declaring that there is room in sports for men and women.

Duh.

But Armour doesn't appear interested in making room. She needs a permanent crisis with permanent victims and permanent villains.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

If misogyny in sports ever fades, so does the need for a professional misogyny detector.

So, when the supply runs low, Nancy Armour manufactures more.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV receives 'symbolic’ sphere in charity's push for AI to 'protect human dignity'
item.description: Photos show Pope Leo XIV receiving the "Sphere of Humanity" glass sculpture as 70 leaders prepare to draft the Codex Humanitatis on AI ethics.
item.content:encoded:
A charity presented Pope Leo XIV with a unique piece of artwork in its push to "protect human dignity" and establish "what should stay human in the age of AI," an official told Fox News Digital.

Photos released by Saint Peter for Humanity captured the pope receiving the "Sphere of Humanity" — a green, Murano glass sculpture that "incorporates handwritten passages from his first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, reflecting on human dignity, vulnerability, solidarity, conscience and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence" — during his General Audience in early September.

The presentation came as Saint Peter for Humanity said it is gearing up next week to gather 70 leaders in New York City to "begin drafting the Codex Humanitatis, an independent initiative inspired by Pope Leo XIV’s call to safeguard human dignity as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly powerful and influential in people’s lives."

"We recognize the benefits of AI. We just believe again that there is another force that should belong to that conversation, that other force is humanity," Olivier Francois, the organization’s president and chairman, told Fox News Digital. "So the Codex Humanitatis, which is our initiative, starts from that simple idea. AI should serve people, protect human dignity, expand human potential and advance common good."

POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL

"So what are we going to do in New York? We are going to gather 70 Nobel laureates, artists, thinkers, philanthropists, technology and AI experts, obviously that's important, and we will ask them maybe the hardest question of our times, you know, as artificial intelligence grows even more powerful, what must remain human?" Francois added. "So obviously, before we head over to machines, we should be clear about what we value most in ourselves. So we will try to define what being human means and what should stay human in the age of AI. So this is a little bit of the initiative we shared with Pope Leo while presenting the sphere and this symbolic gift."

The sphere, based on an original design by Italian architect and designer Gae Aulenti, contains four handwritten passages from Pope Leo XIV’s Magnifica Humanitas, including, "In the era of artificial intelligence, when human dignity is threatened by new forms of dehumanization, ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human."

The pope wrote in the encyclical released in May, "Each generation inherits the task of shaping its own era, of guiding history to become a place where the dignity of every person is safeguarded, justice is promoted and fraternity is made possible," yet "every era also runs the risk of creating an inhumane and more unjust world.

OPINION: POPE LEO XIV’S AI WARNING SPEAKS DIRECTLY TO HOLLYWOOD’S MORAL CRISIS

"For AI to respect human dignity and truly serve the common good, responsibility must be clearly defined at every stage: from those who design and develop these systems to those who use them and rely on them for concrete decisions," the pope wrote. "In many cases, however, the internal processes leading to a result remain opaque, making it harder to assign responsibility and correct errors. This is where accountability becomes crucial: the possibility of identifying who must ‘account’ for decisions, justify them, monitor them, and, when necessary, challenge them and remedy any harm caused.

"Calling for prudence, rigorous evaluation and even, at times, a slower pace in adopting AI does not mean opposing progress; instead, it is an exercise of responsible care for the human family. This need is all the more urgent given the frequent imbalance between the speed of technological growth and the slower development of awareness, norms, safeguards and institutions capable of governing its effects," the pope also said. "It is not enough to invoke ethics in the abstract; robust legal frameworks, independent oversight, informed users and a political system that does not abdicate its responsibility are required. Otherwise, change will be governed only by technocratic thinking and presented as necessary and inevitable, ultimately imposing rules shaped by those who control data, infrastructure and computing power."

Saint Peter for Humanity said in a statement about its New York gathering, "Working across ten groups, participants will develop a first draft of the Codex focused on issues including the future of work, accountability, information integrity, human oversight and the protection of children and families."

"The draft will then enter a global consultation process before being refined into a final set of principles. Saint Peter for Humanity plans to engage governments, companies and institutions in translating those principles into practice, including through engagement at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos," the nonprofit added.

item.title: Harris joins forces with radical Senate nominee in key swing state as 2028 whispers swirl
item.description: Kamala Harris joins Abdul El-Sayed at a Michigan fundraiser on Black maternal health, raising questions about a potential 2028 presidential run.
item.content:encoded:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is set to join Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed at an upcoming roundtable in Michigan, according to his campaign.

The two will appear at a Black maternal health roundtable next Tuesday, raising questions about whether Harris might be trying to court the progressive wing of the party in preparation for a 2028 presidential run.

"I’m just really looking forward to having her here, and she is somebody who so many folks in communities like Detroit look up to as an inspirational leader," El-Sayed told Politico in an interview on Wednesday.

DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN

"I’m grateful that she’s coming in and having conversations about what it takes to get the turnout up, so that we can get on to working on some of these issues in the U.S. Senate," he continued.

The scheduled roundtable comes after Harris endorsed El-Sayed last month, praising his stance on issues like affordability.

"Dr. Abdul El-Sayed understands the power is with the people, and that the stakes couldn’t be higher in this election. While Michiganders struggle to afford everyday essentials — housing, gas, groceries, health care and child care — Trump and Republicans in Congress are giving away $1 trillion in tax breaks to the wealthy and powerful," Harris wrote.

"Abdul knows that we need bold solutions to the crises facing America’s working families and he is ready to take on this fight," Harris continued. "I proudly stand with him to ensure we win a Democratic Senate majority in Nov."

The news of Harris' upcoming visit to Michigan comes as The Detroit News, a prominent Michigan newspaper, endorsed El-Sayed's Republican rival, Mike Rogers, for Senate on Wednesday.

"Mike Rogers is the prototype of a United States Senator," the paper said in its endorsement, referencing his 14 years in the House, Army career, and private sector experience dealing with cybersecurity.

On the other hand, the paper skewered El-Sayed for his radical rhetoric, saying he "has worked so hard covering his tracks leading up to this Senate race that it's impossible to know who he really is or where he would stand in the Senate."

"He has deleted social media posts that reportedly called into question his attitude about America in the aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. He's taken down roughly 100 YouTube videos that paint an unflattering picture of him and his cultural views," the paper concluded. "A candidate who feels the need to hide his past from voters is not someone who can be trusted to be the same person after Election Day as he was on the campaign trail."

In addition to Harris' visit, El-Sayed is expected to have a busy final stretch of his campaign before the November election as he attends multiple fundraisers in California and New York. 

In late September, El-Sayed is scheduled to attend a Hollywood fundraiser at the home of George Soros' nephew, Jeffrey Soros, who is a movie producer. In addition to Soros and his wife, the host committee includes several Obama alums, including Crooked Media's "Pod Save America" hosts Tommy Vietor and Jon Favreau. Ben Rhodes, the failed architect of Obama's Iran deal, is also on the host committee.

El-Sayed will also be visiting San Francisco during this West Coast swing.

12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK

Next month, El-Sayed will also be going to New York City to attend a fundraiser hosted by several far-left activists, where the price to attend ranges from $250 to $57,800.

Harris’ endorsement of El-Sayed marks just her second major progressive candidate endorsement in the 2026 midterms. She is also supporting Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in Maine who is backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

Before the midterms, Harris also supported New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who was also DSA-endorsed, but only stated that she "supported the Democrat in the race."

For his own part, El-Sayed has rejected terms like "progressive" and "moderate" and is not backed by the DSA.

But like Mamdani, El-Sayed has made affordability — and the role of government — key pieces of his campaign. In addition to calling for lowering housing costs, he’s advocated for Medicare for All, opposes corporate tax carve-outs, and he supports tuition-free access to higher education.

Harris has also received support from El-Sayed in the past.

Notably, after now-former President Joe Biden dropped out of the 2024 election, El-Sayed called on the party to rally behind Harris, citing her "potential" for leadership.

"Considering all the dangers of the Republican nominee … it’s time for all of us to unite behind Kamala Harris to defeat Trump," El-Sayed wrote in a post in July 2024.

DEMOCRATS WHO ‘NEVER VOTED REPUBLICAN’ BACK ROGERS OVER EL-SAYED IN RAZOR-CLOSE RACE

El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital on whether El-Sayed might support Harris if she decided to run for the White House in 2028.

item.title: Trump wants largest-ever Israeli heavy bomb transfer — but proposal has Congress preparing for $2.8B fight
item.description: The $2.8 billion package includes 40,000 2,000-pound bombs for Israel, drawing fierce opposition from Bernie Sanders and Chris Van Hollen in Congress.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration is preparing a $2.8 billion military aid package for Israel that would include 40,000 heavy bombs, according to multiple reports. It would be the largest proposed transfer of the powerful munitions to Israel in recent years, if it clears Congress.

The proposed package includes 20,000 unguided bombs designed to destroy buildings and bunkers, known as MK-84 bombs; and 20,000 BLU-117 bombs, which are warhead versions fitted with precision-guidance kits — both bombs are 2,000 pounds per unit. Additionally, according to Reuters and The Washington Post, the proposal includes 20,000 much-tougher I-2000 penetrator warheads, which are designed to penetrate concrete or underground facilities before exploding.

The package, which is not yet final, has been informally communicated to congressional committees that review major U.S. arms sales — and it's already drawing opposition from Democratic lawmakers.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is calling on Congress to reject the White House's proposal, and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., vowed that lawmakers will "work to stop it."

HOUSE DEMOCRATS FRACTURE BADLY OVER MASSIE AMENDMENT TO CUT $3.3B IN U.S. AID TO ISRAEL

"The American people are sick and tired of funding Israel's genocide in Gaza," Sanders wrote on social media, accusing the Trump administration of "doubling down" by providing $2.8 billion in bombs to the Israeli government.

"Not acceptable. Congress must reject these agreements."

Van Hollen similarly criticized the proposed package and its use of U.S. taxpayer funds, writing, "How is this America First? We will work to stop it."

The State Department did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Israel's Ministry of Defense declined to weigh-in.

"All foreign arms sales are moving through the appropriate process. We do not comment on pending sales," a senior administration official told Fox News Digital.

Most of the package would be financed through Foreign Military Financing, which uses congressionally appropriated U.S. funds for eligible allies to purchase American-made defense equipment.

If completed, the package would be the largest single sale of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel in recent years. It would exceed a 2025 sale that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The Trump administration approved that nearly $3 billion sale after bypassing the normal congressional review process.

It's unclear whether that bypass could or will be used again this time around.

The weapons were at the center of a previous U.S. policy dispute, as well.

During President Joe Biden's term, his administration paused a shipment of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel in 2024 over concerns of the potential for mass casualties in densely populated Gaza. President Donald Trump lifted that hold after returning to office.

TRUMP CONFIRMS ‘CRAZY’ NETANYAHU CLASH AS QUESTIONS MOUNT OVER PUSH TO HOLD FIRE ON HEZBOLLAH TERRORISTS

The 2,000-pound bombs have multiple variants designed for different targets, including hardened and underground structures.

Israel has used U.S.-made heavy munitions during its military operations in Gaza and Lebanon, while the United States has used similar weapons against hardened targets in previous conflicts.

The proposed transfer comes as Israel remains engaged on multiple fronts.

Israeli forces have continued strikes against Hamas in Gaza despite a fragile ceasefire, while tensions with Hezbollah persist following fighting in Lebanon.

The United States and Israel also conducted military operations against Iran earlier this year.

The package remains at an early stage of the U.S. arms sales process.

Informal congressional notification allows relevant committees to review a proposed transfer before the administration proceeds to formal notification.

If the administration formally notifies Congress, lawmakers would have an opportunity to review the proposal under the Arms Export Control Act and could pursue legislation seeking to block the sale.

item.title: Josh Hawley shoots down prospect of 2028 White House bid, says he has 'no intention' of running: report

HAWLEY TAKES AIM AT 'CORPORATE WELFARE' AFTER GOP-BACKED TAX BREAK BOOSTED CONTROVERSIAL INDUSTRY

THREE NEW COMPANIES FACE JOSH HAWLEY'S INVESTIGATION INTO AI SURVEILLANCE AND VEHICLE TRACKING

HAWLEY RIPS FLOCK'S SPRAWLING SURVEILLANCE WEB AS TEXAS CITIES CUT CAMERAS OVER PRIVACY AND DATA FEARS

Hawley emphasized the importance of conservative religious voters, describing them as "the backbone of this party," according to the Examiner.

So I’d be real careful about trying to marginalize that coalition," he said, according to the outlet.

item.title: Man says meat-only 'lion diet' cleared psoriasis covering 90% of his body, ended decades of depression
item.description: Stephen Lashbrook says the "lion diet" cleared his severe psoriasis and ended decades of depression, but doctors warn the carnivore approach has risks.
item.content:encoded:
A 50-year-old Florida man who says he spent decades battling severe psoriasis, pain and depression credits an extreme "lion diet" with saving his life.

Stephen Lashbrook, of Pensacola, told Fox News Digital that his depression began at just 4 years old. In his teens, it was compounded by chronic pain, sleeplessness and, in his early 20s, he was diagnosed with psoriasis, an immune-mediated skin disease.

"I was probably 90% covered in psoriasis," Lashbrook said. "My body was just one big, giant, itchy, flaky scab."

DOCTORS DIVIDED OVER NEW DIET TREND THAT HAS BABIES LICKING BUTTER AND GUMMING RIBEYE STEAK

Creams, steroids and other medications did not help, he said. Doctors recommended expensive, long-term injections to combat his inflammation, which left Lashbrook feeling hopeless and suicidal.

Then, he came across a TED Talk from Mikhaila Peterson, an influencer and the daughter of Canadian psychologist and author Jordan Peterson, who used a meat-only elimination diet to tackle her own health issues.

"It gave me a whole new lease on life," he said.

RED MEAT CAN HELP YOUR MOOD IF PART OF A HEALTHY, BALANCED DIET, STUDY SUGGESTS

Lashbrook said he initially cut sugar, grains, fruits and vegetables from his diet. 

On Jan. 1, 2024, he committed to the "lion diet," a strict carnivore diet variation centered on ruminant animal meat, "your cow, your buffalo, your lamb, your goat," he told Fox News Digital.

Within a week, Lashbrook said his itching and suicidal thoughts stopped and, within a month, his skin began to clear up and his pain subsided.

"I haven't had one suicidal thought. I haven't had any depression. I haven't had any pain," he said. "All my skin issues cleared up."

RFK JR. CLAIMS HE LOST 20 POUNDS IN 20 DAYS, GAINED MENTAL CLARITY ON EXTREME DIET

His current menu consists of only grass-fed ground beef and steak. 

Lashbrook said he generally eats one meal per day — about 1.5 to 2 pounds of high-fat ground beef usually cooked in an air fryer.

"I feel like I'm reverse aging," he said.

DOCTORS IN TRAINING LEARN COOKING SKILLS TO HELP PATIENTS AMID AMERICA'S CHRONIC DISEASE CRISIS

His reported improvements are based on personal experience. Lashbrook said he has not had follow-up blood work or visited a doctor since changing his diet, preferring to judge the approach by how he feels.

"Everyone's different," he added. "Not everybody needs to be on a lion diet. ... I'm a very specific case."

Dr. Michael Aziz, a New York City-based internist and regenerative medicine specialist, said that while some people may feel better after cutting sugar and ultra-processed foods, that does not establish the carnivore diet as a treatment for psoriasis or other chronic conditions.

"Many people judge this diet by their success, by their weight loss, but they don't look long-term at their lifespan, how it can be affected by those diets," he told Fox News Digital.

One of the main problems, Aziz added, is that carnivore-centered diets lack fiber. 

"They can lead to problems like constipation. They can lead to kidney stones. They can lead to increased risks for heart attack and stroke," he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Yet meat- and protein-forward have drawn recent attention online and in the mainstream, especially as people seek to cut out ultra-processed foods.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said he follows a carnivore diet centered on meat and fermented foods, claiming it helped him lose weight and gain mental clarity.

Like Lashbrook, Kennedy has acknowledged that his experience may not be right for everyone, and medical experts have cautioned that long-term effects of the carnivore diet remain unclear.

Lashbrook will share his story this week at Carni-Con, a virtual convention centered around carnivore diets. The event runs from Sept. 18–20 and features doctors, creators and other diet advocates.

"The stories are what's most important," Lashbrook said. 

"If people don't hear that these healings are possible, they're not going to know."

item.title: Memphis mom says Trump brought peace to streets as Democratic DA battles task force oversight
item.description: A petition nearing 10,000 signatures demands DA Steve Mulroy drop his fight against Donald Trump's Memphis Safe Task Force accountability measures.
item.content:encoded:
A Memphis mother says President Donald Trump’s federal crime crackdown silenced the gunfire that years of pleas to local leaders could not and finally allowed her children to play outside.

"For once, I’m walking to my mailbox and it’s quiet," Dalisia Ballinger told Fox News Digital. "I’m hearing the birds chirp. I’m hearing the birds sing. I’m seeing children play in the middle of the street. I’m seeing fathers playing football."

The striking turnaround turned Ballinger, a former journalist and violent-crime victim, into one of the most outspoken supporters of the Memphis Safe Task Force as the operation marks one year on the ground.

It also put her at the center of a growing clash with Shelby County District Attorney Steve Mulroy, a Democrat whose lawsuit against two new state oversight laws has sparked a petition demanding that he abandon the legal fight and disclose how his office handles cases generated by the task force.

FORMER CHICAGO DETECTIVE SAYS ONE CITY'S MURDER PLUNGE OFFERS WINDY CITY CRIME BLUEPRINT

"Public safety should not be up for debate," Ballinger said. "I don’t care if you are a Republican. I don’t care if you are a Democrat."

Trump established the multi-agency operation through a presidential memorandum on Sept. 15, 2025, ordering federal, state and local authorities to coordinate against street and violent crime in Memphis. The task force is led by the U.S. Marshals Service and includes mobilized members of the Tennessee National Guard.

The White House said Tuesday that the operation had produced 12,747 arrests as of Sept. 15, including 131 homicide arrests, 1,276 firearms arrests and 1,408 arrests of known gang members. 

The administration also credited the task force with taking 2,160 illegal guns off the streets and recovering 189 missing children.

FBI ANNOUNCES 305 ARRESTS, 24 MISSING CHILDREN RECOVERED IN CHICAGO DURING OPERATION NEW DAWN

Overall crime in Memphis fell nearly 36% compared with the previous year, while murders dropped 36%, robberies fell 42% and vehicle thefts plunged 57%, according to figures released by the White House. City data had already shown crime falling before the task force arrived, and the statistics do not establish how much of the decline resulted directly from the federal surge.

"That era is over. President Trump rejected the excuses, restored law and order, and once again proved that decline is a choice," the White House said.

FBI REPORTS LARGEST DROP IN VIOLENT CRIME AND MURDER SINCE 1937 AS HOMICIDES FALL MORE THAN 18%

Ballinger said the change became personal when her children could play outdoors without the constant fear that had gripped her neighborhood.

She recalled a shooting four houses away in which she said roughly 30 gunshots struck a home occupied by a grandmother and her grandchildren. The family never returned, she said, leaving the property overtaken by grass and weeds.

TRUMP'S DC CRIME CRACKDOWN 'WORKING' AS CITY SEES HOMICIDES PLUMMET 43% SINCE 2025: SLAIN INTERN'S MOM

"We’ve been begging for years for our local leaders for assistance and for help," Ballinger said. "My children deserve peace, and with the Memphis Safe Task Force being here, we’ve finally been able to get that peace."

Now, she and other supporters argue the operation’s arrests mean little if prosecutors later reduce or dismiss cases without explaining why.

PROSECUTOR OUSTED AFTER ALLEGED ROMANCE WITH ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SEX-CRIME SUSPECT: 'PATTERN OF MISCONDUCT'

A Change.org petition titled "Stop Memphis DA From Protecting Criminals" had gathered nearly 10,000 verified signatures Wednesday. 

The petition calls on Mulroy to drop a May lawsuit challenging the Memphis Safe Task Force Accountability Act and a separate law that authorizes the Tennessee attorney general to audit his office’s decisions in task force cases.

The accountability law requires Mulroy’s office to submit a report every 10 business days when it settles or dismisses a charge arising from the task force. The second law allows the state attorney general to review prosecutorial decisions in those cases and ask the Tennessee Supreme Court to appoint a temporary prosecutor.

PRIMARY SHOWDOWN: CONSERVATIVE FIREBRAND MARSHA BLACKBURN EYES GOVERNOR'S OFFICE IN TENNESSEE

Mulroy argues that both laws unconstitutionally single out Shelby County, intrude on the discretion of a locally elected prosecutor and burden his staff with duplicative reporting. His office said it already reports case outcomes under existing Tennessee law.

"These bills target Shelby County unfairly and infringe on the rights of Shelby County voters," Mulroy said when the lawsuit was filed. He has characterized the dispute as a battle over whether Shelby County voters or state officials in Nashville control the district attorney’s office.

Petition supporters see the lawsuit differently.

"Thanks to President Trump, the Memphis Safe Task Force has delivered more for this city in one year than anyone thought possible," Ballinger, one of the petition's leading voices, said in a statement. "While federal, state, and local agents risk their lives taking criminals off our streets, DA Mulroy is fighting in court to hide how his office is undermining this task force."

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., and Tennessee state Sen. Brent Taylor previously pressed Mulroy for details after his office reported that 430 of 514 felony cases resolved in December 2025 ended without prison time and that 166 of the cases were categorized as violent. The lawmakers said the figures left unanswered how many defendants in violent cases received no prison sentence. Mulroy has accused his Republican critics of distorting crime data for political purposes.

Ballinger rejected the claim that the petition is merely a partisan campaign against a Democratic prosecutor.

"We have children. We have regular people that might not even be into politics," she said. "We deserve peace. Whether it’s on the East Coast, the West Coast or South, we all deserve peace."

MISSISSIPPI DISTRICT ATTORNEY JODY OWENS RESIGNS AFTER PLEADING GUILTY IN FEDERAL BRIBERY CASE: REPORT

The task force has also drawn fierce opposition. The ACLU of Tennessee and several Memphis residents have accused agents of aggressive policing and retaliation against people who record law enforcement.

Four residents filed a federal lawsuit this year alleging harassment, unlawful arrests and physical mistreatment while exercising their First Amendment rights.

The allegations have not been proven in court, while task force supporters point to thousands of arrests and sharply falling crime numbers as evidence the operation is working.

Ballinger said legitimate complaints should be reviewed, but she does not believe they justify dismantling an operation she credits with making her neighborhood livable again.

"I’m all for fairness, and I’m all for law and order," she said. "If we need to go back to the table [and] restructure so that people can feel safe, we can definitely put that on the board."

For Ballinger, the anniversary is measured less by government statistics than by what she can see and hear beyond her front door.

"It was noticeably enough to where it’s like, ‘Wow, there’s kids actually outside playing,’" she said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mulroy’s office for comment.

item.title: The Fed just threw a wrench in Trump's midterm economic message
item.description: Kevin Warsh's first rate hike as Fed chair defies President Donald Trump's repeated push for lower borrowing costs ahead of midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
With the midterms looming, President Donald Trump wants lower interest rates to ease the squeeze on American families. Instead, the Federal Reserve raised rates on Wednesday.

The decision is aimed at combating stubborn inflation, but it will make borrowing more expensive for voters and delivers a big hit to Trump's economic promises with less than two months until Americans cast their ballots and determine which party will control Congress.

The Fed does not set the prices of groceries, cars or homes. But its decisions affect how much Americans pay to borrow money, especially when they buy a house or car. Higher rates can add hundreds of dollars to monthly payments, even when the price of the home or vehicle has not changed.

ONE LITTLE-KNOWN MEETING HELPS DECIDE WHAT AMERICANS CAN AFFORD — AND WHAT THEY CAN’T

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised the federal funds rate by a quarter of a percentage point Wednesday, bringing it to a range of 3.75% to 4%. The increase — the Fed’s first in three years — was aimed at slowing inflation, which remains above the central bank’s 2% goal. Higher energy prices and tariffs have added to pressure on household budgets, and the Fed’s projections indicate that another rate increase could come later this year if inflation remains elevated.

The rate hike puts Kevin Warsh, Trump’s pick to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, at odds with the president’s push for lower borrowing costs.

The decision could strain their relationship and revive memories of Trump’s repeated clashes with former Fed Chair Jerome Powell.

TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE

Although the president appoints members of the Fed’s Board of Governors, the FOMC is designed to make rate decisions based on economic conditions rather than political pressure.

Warsh underscored that independence Wednesday, saying the Fed acted based on its assessment of employment, the strength of the economy and the inflation outlook.

WARSH FACES FIRST BIG TEST ON CAPITOL HILL AS TRUMP’S FED VISION COMES INTO FOCUS

The Fed chairman was later asked what message he had for Trump, who has repeatedly called for lower rates.

He declined to discuss the president, saying, "I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

For Trump, the timing is difficult.

He campaigned on improving affordability, but the rate increase could make it harder for households to feel financial relief — and for the administration to show voters that its economic promises are producing results. With affordability and the cost of living already central issues in the midterm elections, higher borrowing costs could further complicate the president’s economic message.

item.title: Dem megadonor unleashes reality check on Harris for 2028 while eying socialist firebrand
item.description: Reid Hoffman, a top Silicon Valley donor, calls another Kamala Harris 2028 presidential run a "very challenging path" while expressing surprising openness to supporting Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
item.content:encoded:
One of Kamala Harris' biggest billionaire backers in 2024 is already casting doubt on another White House bid — while showing surprising openness to a potential 2028 contender from a very different corner of the Democratic Party.

LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman called another Harris presidential run a "very challenging path" Wednesday before leaving the door open to supporting Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and describing the progressive firebrand as "pragmatic."

"It depends a little bit," Hoffman said when asked during POLITICO's Decoded Summit Wednesday in the nation's capital whether he would support Ocasio-Cortez for a 2028 run. "I think she's much more pragmatic than people give her credit for."

The comments mark a notable contrast for Hoffman, who poured millions of dollars into helping elect Harris in 2024 and rallied other Silicon Valley donors behind her campaign after former President Joe Biden ended his re-election bid. Asked Wednesday whether Harris should try again in 2028, Hoffman pointed to what he expects to be a crowded Democratic field.

WATCH: AOC WON'T RULE OUT WHITE HOUSE BID AFTER POLL NAMES HER DEMOCRATS' TOP 2028 PICK

"I think it would be a very challenging path for her, and it's going to be a very noisy field," Hoffman said in response.

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

Hoffman's answer was not an endorsement, however. He said any potential support for Ocasio-Cortez would depend in part on whom she was running against, before Hoffman laid out the qualities he would look for in a candidate.

"If you're basically kind of pro-society, which she is, and pro-business, which is a question, that tends to be where I think the right focal points are," Hoffman said.

Meanwhile, two years earlier, Hoffman had made a similar case for Harris, pitching her to hundreds of venture capitalists as "a great centrist" who cared about both society and business, according to a report from The Washington Post. 

"She is a great centrist in that she cares about a greater society and cares about business," Hoffman said during a virtual "VCs for Harris" rally in 2024, according to The Washington Post.

Hoffman’s comments this week about Harris' potential 2028 bid also came days after California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he would not seek the presidency if Harris entered the 2028 race. 

Republican strategist Mark Bednar, who previously worked for then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, interpreted the two developments as early signs of uncertainty surrounding Harris' position in the emerging Democratic field.

GAVIN NEWSOM SAYS HE WON'T RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 IF KAMALA HARRIS RUNS

"The idea of pouring cold water over Kamala for others to step forward seems to be very real," Bednar told Fox News Digital. "I don't know if it's directly connected to Newsom in that instance, but it's super interesting how it happens the day after."

Bednar, meanwhile, described Newsom's comments about his potential 2028 presidential run as a "smoke signal to Democratic donors" that "you guys are going to have to be the ones that be the bad cop here because I'm just going to be the good cop in public."

"If you read between the lines, he's signaling to his donors and to his prospective donors, ‘Hey, you guys need to do the dirty work to get her out of the race,’" Bednar said.

Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Harris, Ocasio-Cortez and Hoffman, but did not receive a response in time for publication.

item.title: Scammers are coming for your money. Here’s the one thing you must never do
item.description: Phone spoofing lets scammers impersonate your bank with the correct caller ID and account details. These critical steps can help prevent identity theft.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine getting a phone call from your bank. The bank's name is listed on the caller ID with the correct phone number. They know key details about you — your name, your account numbers, maybe even your Social Security number or mother's maiden name.

They warn you that you have fallen victim to a financial scam. But the plot twist is that they are the scammers!

YOUR FAMILY COULD BE ONE PHONE CALL FROM A BANK SCAM

This is happening across the country at an alarming rate.

Technology can help increase our productivity, but it can also boost scammers by enabling increasingly sophisticated tactics that allow them to impersonate companies, access sensitive information and create a panic that causes even the savviest people to unwittingly help them complete their scams.

FRAUD EXPERT WARNS AI IS HELPING CRIMINALS OUTPACE THE GOVERNMENT: 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT TOOLS'

So, how can you protect yourself from these growing scams, including those in which the scammer is impersonating your bank?

If you see your bank, credit card company, Amazon, Microsoft or any other company with whom you do business calling, and you aren't immediately expecting that call, do not answer your phone.

Scammers are "spoofing" phone numbers so that the phone number shows up on your phone with the name of a big company even though they are not affiliated with it. Sometimes, it even shows the correct phone number even though they are calling from another number.

If you don't answer your phone, you take away a huge tool for scammers: their ability to create urgency and panic. When you are told that you are the subject of fraud, that your money is at risk, or something similar, and you need to take action, you panic.

APPLE PAY TEXT SCAM THREATENS $8,250 LOSS IN 35 MINUTES

In a state of panic, you do not think clearly, and this can lead you to take actions that you would never undertake in a calm state.

I personally suggest not answering any phone calls. If you receive a call, try calling the person or business back using the number in your contacts if they leave a message.

AMAZON'S ALEXA CAN NOW VERIFY SUSPICIOUS MESSAGES

If you get a voicemail message about an issue (such as supposedly being the victim of a scam) or a text or email, again, do not panic.

Instead, find a trusted touchpoint.

THE SCAM TEXT TEST: SPOT DANGER BEFORE YOU TAP

For banks, credit card companies and other financial providers, find their phone number on the back of your bank card or on an old paper statement that you know is legitimate.

You can also go to their website and look for a phone number or customer service email address.

HI MOM TEXT SCAM: HOW TO SPOT FAKE EMERGENCY TEXTS

This puts you in control of the contact, and you can safely find out if there is legitimately an issue or if you have been contacted by a scammer.

Controlling the contact instead of letting the scammer be in control is key to fighting scams.

If you do let a text or phone call break through (and you shouldn't, but I know it happens), do not respond or give out sensitive information in response to their requests.

For example, they may send you a text and ask for a security code sent to your phone.

Again, this is them trying to scam you, not help you. Giving up codes like this could help them drain your bank account.

Instead, again, seek out a trusted phone number and call the company to verify whether there is a problem. If there is, they can help you directly. Much of the time, you will find out it was a scam attempt.

Creating urgency is key for scammers. They make you worried. As noted above, you get into a state of panic, and you take action without thinking.

If you are asked to take any urgent action, such as going to a bank immediately, withdrawing or moving funds, buying gift cards, immediately giving out information or anything else, stop and take a beat.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The same goes for secrecy. If they tell you not to contact the police or not to tell the bank teller what is going on because they might be in on it, do not listen. You are not James Bond, and you are not caught up in an international stakeout — you are simply a person whom a fraudster is trying to trick.

Reset and call your financial institution or the police for guidance.

This may sound obvious while you are reading it, but thousands of well-meaning people have fallen victim to the psychological manipulation of scammers.

Finally, with AI technology, even voices are being spoofed. Have a family code phrase among your family members that isn't published anywhere. Then, if someone calls using your loved one's voice as part of a scam, you can ask for the code phrase. If it isn't given, you will know it is not your family member.

Scammers are everywhere. They are relentless, and they will stop at nothing to try to fleece you. Be diligent, take control of your communications and defuse urgency so that they do not succeed.
